methods.short: 27 real local-model calls: three synthetic SQLite cases × three coordination modes × three calls. Every call sees the same complete evidence for its case. Stored transcripts are brief generated conclusions, not hidden reasoning.
methods.protocol: Solo: one investigator revises its own prior summaries. Independent: three isolated investigators vote; at least two matching valid answers required. Relay: analyst, critic and adjudicator see prior summaries. All modes receive the same frozen SQL evidence; this is a coordination exercise, not autonomous tool use.

budget.fairness: Same call count, generation caps, model and evidence access. Input tokens, actual output tokens, role instructions and elapsed time differ. No equal-total-token or equal-cost claim.

limitations: One small quantized local model and three hand-built cases; these results are not a benchmark or evidence of a generally superior architecture.
One deterministic seed schedule per mode; no repeated trials or uncertainty interval.
SQL evidence is precomputed and supplied in full. Models cite query IDs but do not choose or execute tools.
Confidence is an uncalibrated self-report. Exact answer scoring does not certify every sentence of a rationale.
Mode order and caching affect latency; durations are observations, not controlled speed comparisons.
Same seed and digest aid reproduction but backend/platform differences can change generated text.

cases.title: The doubled revenue
cases.question: Why does the new dashboard report twice the revenue of the order ledger?
cases.brief: A dashboard release changed the reporting query to join customer history. The ledger is the source of truth for booked order amounts. An operator suspects a successful promotion. Diagnose the discrepancy, not the promotion itself.

hypotheses.title: Real sales growth explains the discrepancy
The history join counts each order twice
Duplicate order IDs inflate the ledger

answer.explanation: Each order joins two customer-version rows. Filtering the current version restores the source ledger total; order IDs are unique and source revenue is unchanged between days.

queries.title: Ledger and new dashboard totals
queries.sql: SELECT o.day, COUNT(*) AS joined_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) AS distinct_orders, SUM(o.amount) AS dashboard_revenue, (SELECT SUM(b.amount) FROM orders b WHERE b.day=o.day) AS ledger_revenue FROM orders o JOIN customer_versions c ON o.customer_id=c.customer_id GROUP BY o.day ORDER BY o.day

queries.title: Customer history multiplicity
queries.sql: SELECT version, current, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM customer_versions GROUP BY version,current ORDER BY version

queries.title: Repaired join and source uniqueness
queries.sql: SELECT o.day, COUNT(*) AS joined_rows, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue, (SELECT COUNT(*)-COUNT(DISTINCT id) FROM orders b WHERE b.day=o.day) AS duplicate_source_ids FROM orders o JOIN customer_versions c ON o.customer_id=c.customer_id AND c.current=1 GROUP BY o.day ORDER BY o.day

cases.title: The falling conversion rate
cases.question: Why does total conversion fall while both device groups improve?
cases.brief: A product report shows a large drop in conversion after a campaign. Every session has exactly one tracking record and a verified conversion label. Explain the aggregate change using the supplied groups.

hypotheses.title: Conversion worsened within both device groups
Tracking loss creates an artificial decline
Traffic moved toward the lower-converting device group

answer.explanation: The mobile share rises from 10% to 90%. Mobile converts less than desktop in both periods, even though each group improves. The weighted overall rate falls from 9.2% to 3.8%; the data contain no tracking loss.

queries.title: Overall conversion
queries.sql: SELECT period, COUNT(*) AS sessions, SUM(converted) AS conversions, ROUND(100.0*AVG(converted),2) AS conversion_percent FROM sessions GROUP BY period ORDER BY period DESC

queries.title: Conversion and volume by device
queries.sql: SELECT period, device, COUNT(*) AS sessions, SUM(converted) AS conversions, ROUND(100.0*AVG(converted),2) AS conversion_percent FROM sessions GROUP BY period,device ORDER BY period DESC,device

queries.title: Tracking integrity
queries.sql: SELECT period, SUM(tracked) AS tracked, COUNT(*) AS total, COUNT(*)-COUNT(DISTINCT id) AS duplicate_ids FROM sessions GROUP BY period ORDER BY period DESC

cases.title: The overnight demand scare
cases.question: Why did the midnight dashboard show a 60% drop that disappeared the next morning?
cases.brief: All timestamps are UTC. Daily demand is defined by event time. The first snapshot was taken just before 2026-10-12 00:00 UTC; the next was taken at 02:00. An operator suspects a demand collapse. Identify the demonstrated reporting cause.

hypotheses.title: Late arrivals made the first snapshot incomplete
Duplicate source IDs made the morning count rebound

answer.explanation: Both days contain 100 unique event-time records in the completed dataset. Sixty of the second day’s records arrived after the first snapshot and before the second. No source IDs are duplicated.

queries.title: Counts available at the first snapshot
queries.sql: SELECT DATE(event_at) AS event_day, COUNT(*) AS available FROM events WHERE arrived_at < '2026-10-12 00:00:00' GROUP BY DATE(event_at) ORDER BY event_day

queries.title: Counts at 02:00 and late arrivals
queries.sql: SELECT DATE(event_at) AS event_day, COUNT(*) AS available_at_02, SUM(arrived_at >= '2026-10-12 00:00:00') AS arrived_after_first_snapshot FROM events WHERE arrived_at < '2026-10-12 02:00:00' GROUP BY DATE(event_at) ORDER BY event_day

queries.title: Time range and source uniqueness
queries.sql: SELECT DATE(event_at) AS event_day, MIN(event_at) AS first_event, MAX(event_at) AS last_event, COUNT(*)-COUNT(DISTINCT id) AS duplicate_ids FROM events GROUP BY DATE(event_at) ORDER BY event_day
